pv.s2c: If PulseCheck meets an unexpected error, it saves technical details in a log file in the PulseCheck folder of your local app data. Nothing is sent. If you report a problem, check the file before sharing it, as it can contain file paths.
q8: Windows or my browser blocks the download. What can I do?
a8: In Edge or Chrome, open the downloads list, click the three dots next to the file, choose Keep, then Show more and Keep anyway. When you run it, if Windows says it protected your PC, click More info then Run anyway. You can also right-click the file, choose Properties and tick Unblock. If Windows 11 Smart App Control is on, it blocks every unsigned app and cannot be bypassed. The file is not code-signed yet; you can check it with the hash on the release page.
sol3.d: Your graphics card (A) and your 1440p 144 Hz screen (B) call for a class 7 card. Each suggestion shows its reasons, a cost range and what to check first, such as the power supply.
sol.lead: Tell PulseCheck what you use the PC for. It compares your hardware with your screen and your usage, then explains what to change, in order of value.
pv.s2b: The Solutions tab works entirely on your PC from the information above. It contains no advertising and no affiliate links, and your hardware list is never sent anywhere.
q7: Will it tell me which graphics card or memory to buy?
sol2.d: Graphics presets matched to your card and your display, with the right upscaler (DLSS, FSR or XeSS) and a sensible frame cap.
sol1.d: Refresh rate stuck at 60 Hz, memory below its rated speed, an old graphics driver, too many startup programs. Many have a Fix button that shows what it will change and asks you first; the others show the exact menu to open.
sol.alt: PulseCheck Solutions tab with upgrade suggestions and the reasons behind them
a7: Yes. After a scan, the Solutions tab compares your graphics card, processor, memory, drives and screen with your usage (gaming, video and 3D, work, development) and explains what is worth upgrading and why. Performance classes are estimates, and there are no ads or affiliate links, so compare current reviews and prices before buying.

q1: Is it safe? What does it send?
a1: Nothing is uploaded and there is no telemetry. PulseCheck reads information from your PC and saves a report only where you choose. Its network tests contact public servers: ping, DNS, one small web request and an optional 10 MB speed test. The privacy policy lists them all.
q2: Does it change anything on my PC?
a2: Scanning never changes anything. If you press Fix, PulseCheck shows exactly what it will do and asks you to confirm. Most changes can be undone from the app, and a record is kept on your PC. It never installs software or touches your antivirus or firewall.
q3: Can it tell whether a PC is used or refurbished?
a3: It shows signs, such as battery wear or a missing activation. These are indicators, not proof.
a4: Not for most checks. Choose Run as administrator for the TPM check and a few others.
a5: Yes. It is free and open source under the MIT license, with no ads and no paid tier.

pv.title: Privacy policy
pv.s1.p: PulseCheck runs on your PC. It does not collect, store or send your personal data to us or to anyone else. There are no accounts, no analytics and no advertising.
pv.s2.p: To run its checks, the app reads information about your computer: hardware and operating system details, drive and battery status, security settings, names of installed software, event log summaries and network configuration. This information stays on your PC. It appears in the app window and, only if you choose Save report, in an HTML file that you save yourself. The report includes your computer name, so remove it before sharing if you prefer.
pv.s3.h: What the app sends over the network
pv.s3.p: Only the connection test uses the network. It contacts public servers and sends no information about you or your PC beyond what any internet connection reveals, such as your IP address.
pv.n1: Ping to your router, to 1.1.1.1 (Cloudflare) and to 8.8.8.8 (Google)
pv.n2: A DNS lookup and an HTTPS connection to www.microsoft.com
pv.n3: One small request to www.msftconnecttest.com to detect captive portals
pv.n4: Optional: a 10 MB download from speed.cloudflare.com for the speed test
pv.s4.p: Scanning changes nothing. If you press Fix and confirm, PulseCheck applies only the change it announced: a Windows setting for your account, a startup entry, temporary files, or a Microsoft Store app you ticked. It never installs software and never changes your antivirus or firewall. Each change is recorded in a log file in the PulseCheck folder of your local app data, and most changes can be undone from the app.
pv.s5.p: This site is hosted on GitHub Pages. It uses no cookies, no analytics and no third-party fonts or scripts. GitHub, as the host, may process technical data such as IP addresses under its own privacy statement. Downloads are served by GitHub Releases.
pv.s6.p: The complete source code is public, so every statement above can be checked. For questions or concerns, open an issue:
pv.s7.p: If this policy changes, the new version is published here with a new date.
